title: Another person dies in RCMP custody
article: Another Yukon man has died in the custody of the RCMP, this time in Watson Lake.
Freddie Stewart, 36, died in the Watson Lake police detachment cell after being arrested for public intoxication at about 12:15 a.m. Saturday.
Stewart was arrested outside Tags Food and Gas and brought to the Watson Lake detachment and put in a cell.
At 2:38 a.m., officers found Stewart apparently not breathing. CPR was started immediately in an attempt to resuscitate Stewart, but all efforts to revive him were unsuccessful.
An ambulance was dispatched and Stewart was taken to the Watson Lake Hospital. There, at 4:12 a.m., he was pronounced dead by the attending doctor.
This death is the second in RCMP cells in the past three months.
Last Dec. 25, another Watson Lake man, John Tibbett Jr., 38, was found dead in his Whitehorse RCMP cell, having hung himself.
In March 1995, 40-year-old Robert Keddie died while in the custody of the Whitehorse RCMP. A drug overdose complicated by alcohol consumption was blamed for his death.
Like Tibbett and Stewart, Keddie was originally arrested on an alcohol-related charge.
Stewart's cell did have a camera, and a guard was on duty.
Both the Yukon coroner and the RCMP will hold separate investigations into the incident, though foul play is not suspected.
Any coroner's inquest is at least several months away.
Two other inquests are still to be held for individuals who were either in RCMP holding cells or Whitehorse Correctional Centre cells at the time of their deaths.
Besides Tibbett, Jolie Angelina McNabb hung herself in the Whitehorse jail last Sept. 3.
An autopsy on Stewart will be performed in Vancouver by Dr. Laurel Gray, after which more information will be made available, possibly as soon as tomorrow morning.
Stewart, who would have celebrated his 37th birthday on Sunday, was known to police and had a long history of minor, non-violent offences.
Pat Irvin, owner of most of the bars in Watson Lake, also knew Stewart.
"He was not allowed to drink in any of our bars," he said in an interview this morning. "He might come in to socialize, but as soon as he becomes a nuisance, he's out. We don't serve him."
Irvin went on to say that Stewart was more of a pest than a threat.
When contacted by the Star, neither the Watson Lake Hospital nor the ambulance dispatch service were in a position to comment.
Nor were the RCMP, who are waiting for more information to come in before making any further statements.
